hook.text: A gas engine has hundreds of moving parts. An electric motor has about 20. Fewer parts mean fewer jobs.

buildup.text: Transmission plants, exhaust system factories, and engine foundries face shutdown as EVs scale.

discovery.text: New jobs emerge in battery manufacturing, charging infrastructure, and software development.

twist.text: But the new jobs aren't always in the same places or for the same workers as the old ones.

climax.text: Governments are racing to retrain workers and attract battery factories to displaced communities.

punchline.text: EVs create jobs—just not for everyone who loses one.

quiz.question: Why do EVs require fewer manufacturing workers?
options: They have far fewer moving parts

details.summary: The shift from combustion engines to electric drivetrains threatens millions of jobs in engine manufacturing, fuel stations, and maintenance shops while creating new roles in battery production and software.
details.whyItMatters: Electric cars have far fewer parts and need less maintenance, eliminating many traditional automotive jobs. Managing this workforce transition is critical to avoiding social and economic disruption.
takeaways: EVs have 80 percent fewer moving parts than combustion cars
Engine and transmission plants face closure or conversion
Battery gigafactories are creating new manufacturing jobs

faq.question: How many jobs could be lost in the transition to EVs?
faq.answer: Studies estimate millions of jobs worldwide in engine manufacturing, fuel distribution, and vehicle maintenance are at risk. Germany alone estimates 400,000 auto-related jobs could be affected by the EV transition.

faq.question: Do battery factories create as many jobs as engine plants?
faq.answer: Not directly. Battery manufacturing is more automated and requires fewer workers per unit of production. However, the entire EV ecosystem including charging, software, and recycling creates new job categories.
